newsitem.title: CROATIA: German firm helps Croatian companies restructure.
newsitem.headline: German firm helps Croatian companies restructure.

text.p: German consultancy Carl Duisberg Gesellschaft (CDG) has helped Croatia restructure six ailing companies, officials and experts said on Tuesday.

Croatian government officials at a news conference described a pilot project designed to aid medium-sized firms from three key industrial sectors as "vital" in reorganising their business in order to face challenges of a market economy.
"This was invaluable help, particularly since it came at a time when effects of the war were still strongly felt," said Tomislav Druzak, president of the Croatian Privatisation Fund.
The first six represent only a fraction of the economy, but many other companies from all sectors were also said to be interested in implementing similar restructuring measures under CDG's guidance.

The firms included in the pilot project are textile makers Modea from Garesnica and Tekstilni Kombinat Zagreb, food firms PPK Kutjevo and PPK Velebit, and wood-processing plant Bilokalnik and oak furniture maker Spacva from Vinkovci.
Some of them were situated right next to war zones during the 1991-95 conflict with Croatia's separatist Serbs and were forced to cut production, leaving some capacities underemployed.
Transport of raw materials and finished products from relatively isolated areas presented a huge problem and increased their already huge costs, officials said.
Among many problems that plagued these firms, they also cited excess workforce, dated technology, low productivity and poor management training.
Lack of a coherent business strategy, necessary to expand production and win new markets in place of those lost in the breakup of former Yugoslavia, only added to their aggravation.
When indepth restructuring of these firms began in 1996, they were contolled by the state privatisation agency because teetering on the brink of collapse they were not too attractive to investors.
Revamped, they are now much closer to an evenual sell-off and should have no difficulty finding buyers, privatisation officials said.
But Heinz Bernd Windscheidt said the help of CDG stopped short of advising these firms about privatisation.
"We approach them from another angle, providing a different kind of expertise," he told Reuters.

Although much still remains to be done including sizeable investment into expanding production capacities of mostly overahauled firms and their full computerisation, directors said they as much further along a path to profitability.
Project managers from individual firms were said to have acquired valuable knowledge through their overhaul which could qualify them for advising other firms on how to reorganise.
"We have undergone in-house training and have implemented strict cost planning. Our productivity and output are rising," said Mladen Plantic of Zagreb's Tekstilni Kombinat.
